items.note: Variant of 'studies show' not in uncited-authority.ts; past-perfect form still weasels without citation
items.example: Studies have shown that multitasking reduces productivity.

items.note: Past-perfect variant of 'research shows'; same gap-fill without citation
items.example: Research has shown that sleep deprivation impairs judgment.

items.note: Parallel to 'researchers have found' but uses mass noun; not in existing list
items.example: Research has found that exercise boosts cognitive performance.

items.note: Studies-as-plural-agent with 'found'; not covered by existing patterns
items.example: Studies have found a strong link between stress and heart disease.

items.note: Passive-authority construction; asserts consensus without any source
items.example: It is widely known that sugar is bad for your teeth.

items.note: Passive consensus claim; not in uncited-authority.ts (covered only as 'it is widely accepted')
items.example: It is widely believed that humans only use ten percent of their brains.

items.note: Rhetorical assertion that something is obvious; signals padding, not evidence
items.example: It is no secret that big tech companies collect personal data.

items.note: Claims the following point is self-evident, avoiding the burden of proof; in prohibited-phrases is absent
items.example: Needless to say, customer satisfaction drives revenue.

items.note: Quantified version of 'experts believe'; not in existing list; 'many believe' is there but this adds the expert framing
items.example: Many experts believe artificial intelligence will reshape the workforce.

items.note: Plural-expert consensus without any named expert
items.example: Many experts agree that climate change is the defining challenge of our time.

items.note: Majority-consensus claim with no source; stronger quantifier than 'many'
items.example: Most experts agree that a balanced diet is essential for good health.

items.note: Domain-scoped vague attribution; slightly more specific than 'experts say' but still unnamed
items.example: Industry experts say the market is poised for rapid growth.

items.note: Prestige-modifier on vague attribution; no source given
items.example: Leading experts say the new treatment could revolutionize care.

items.note: Attribution to research-in-general rather than a named study or author
items.example: According to research, walking daily lowers the risk of diabetes.

items.note: Plural-study attribution with no citation; parallel to 'according to experts'
items.example: According to studies, remote workers are more productive.

items.note: Attributes a specific claim to all of science; no study, no author
items.example: According to science, gratitude journaling reduces anxiety.

items.note: Science personified as authority without citation; related to 'science says' but not the same token sequence
items.example: Science tells us that the human body can go three weeks without food.

items.note: Stronger claim than 'science says'; not in existing list
items.example: Science confirms that meditation reduces cortisol levels.

items.note: Strong certainty claim with passive erasure of who proved it and how
items.example: It has been proven that positive reinforcement outperforms punishment.

items.note: Passive-voice version of 'studies show'; source is completely erased
items.example: It has been shown that sleep affects memory consolidation.

items.note: Passive erasure of who found it; near-identical signal to 'it has been shown'
items.example: It has been found that regular exercise improves mood.

items.note: Claims a consensus has already been settled without naming who settled it
items.example: It has been established that smoking causes lung cancer.

items.note: Passive demonstration claim; no study, no author, no date
items.example: It has been demonstrated that mindfulness reduces workplace stress.

items.note: Softer consensus claim; some FP risk when used in genuine academic hedging, but without citation it's weasel
items.example: It is generally accepted that inflation erodes purchasing power.

items.note: Absolute-consensus claim; rarely true for anything except basic facts, and those don't need attribution
items.example: It is universally accepted that good leadership drives employee engagement.

items.note: Implies shared knowledge without citing where that understanding comes from
items.example: It is commonly understood that first impressions matter in hiring.

items.note: Variant of 'commonly understood'; same passive consensus erasure
items.example: It is generally understood that diet affects mental health.

items.text: it is a well-known fact that
items.note: Double assertion of facthood and fame; classic weasel opener
items.example: It is a well-known fact that exercise reduces the risk of chronic disease.

items.note: Presupposes wide knowledge to avoid stating a source
items.example: As is well known, social media affects teenage mental health.

items.note: Absolute universality claim used as a substitute for evidence
items.example: As everyone knows, money can't buy happiness.

items.note: Inclusive false-consensus framing that excludes counter-evidence by assumption
items.example: As we all know, good nutrition is the foundation of good health.

items.note: Unnamed collective attribution; passive observer framing with no source
items.example: Observers have noted a shift in consumer attitudes toward sustainability.

items.note: Softer hedge variant of 'observers have noted'; same erasure of source
items.example: Observers have suggested the policy may backfire.

items.note: Unnamed analyst attribution; higher FP risk in financial journalism where analysts are a recognized class, but no name still weasels
items.example: Analysts suggest the sector is overvalued.

items.note: Same as 'analysts suggest'; common in finance writing, but unnamed
items.example: Analysts say the company faces headwinds in the coming quarter.

items.note: Belief attribution to unnamed analysts; weakens claim without citation
items.example: Analysts believe the merger will face regulatory hurdles.

items.note: Medical-authority variant of 'experts say'; no named doctor, no source
items.example: Doctors say that sitting for long periods is as harmful as smoking.

items.note: Medical recommendation claim with no named source or guideline
items.example: Doctors recommend getting at least eight hours of sleep per night.

items.note: Domain-scoped vague attribution; 'health' adds specificity veneer without naming anyone
items.example: Health experts say processed food is driving the obesity epidemic.

items.note: Discipline-specific unnamed authority; no individual or body named
items.example: Nutritionists say breakfast is the most important meal of the day.

items.note: Discipline-specific unnamed authority; common in self-help and wellness AI content
items.example: Psychologists say that labeling emotions helps regulate them.

items.note: Domain-scoped attribution; FP risk moderate in economics journalism, but still weasel without a name
items.example: Economists say the tax cut will stimulate growth.

items.note: Prestige-plural unnamed consensus; 'leaders' adds authority without naming them
items.example: Industry leaders agree that AI is the most disruptive technology of the decade.

items.note: Unnamed insider attribution; implies privileged knowledge without any source
items.example: Industry insiders say the launch has been delayed indefinitely.

items.note: Legitimate in journalism when sources require anonymity; FP risk is high; slop only when used in non-journalistic content to avoid citing anything
items.example: Sources say the company is considering layoffs.

items.note: Unnamed researcher attribution with hedged consensus; legitimate in academic hedging but weasel without a citation
items.example: Some researchers argue that social media is a net negative for democracy.

items.note: Fringe-minority framing without naming the scientists
items.example: Some scientists believe consciousness may be a quantum phenomenon.

items.note: Popular-belief claim masquerading as evidence; related to 'many believe' already covered but specifies 'people' explicitly
items.example: Many people believe that vaccines cause autism.

items.text: a growing body of evidence suggests
items.note: Sophisticated-sounding weasel phrase that implies accumulation without citing any single study
items.example: A growing body of evidence suggests that gut health affects mental wellbeing.

items.text: a growing body of research suggests
items.note: Variant of the above with 'research'; both are AI-common gap-filling phrases
items.example: A growing body of research suggests that ultra-processed foods are addictive.

items.note: Claims consensus of the entire scientific community without any evidence or citation
items.example: The scientific community agrees that more funding is needed for mental health research.

items.note: Asserts consensus without citing where it was formed or who holds it
items.example: The consensus is that renewable energy will replace fossil fuels within decades.

items.note: Qualifier 'general' hedges the consensus claim without adding a source
items.example: The general consensus is that remote work improves employee satisfaction.

items.note: Hyperbolic quantity claim for studies; 'countless' asserts volume to substitute for citation
items.example: Countless studies have shown that exercise improves mental health.

items.note: Quantity-inflation variant of 'studies have shown'; implies breadth without citing any study
items.example: Numerous studies have shown that sleep deprivation leads to weight gain.

items.note: Same as above with 'suggest'; hedged version
items.example: Numerous studies suggest that meditation reduces blood pressure.

items.note: Replication claim without naming any of the studies
items.example: Multiple studies have found that social connection reduces mortality risk.

items.note: Evidence used as an agent pointing at a conclusion without any source named; different token sequence from 'evidence shows/suggests'
items.example: Evidence points to a link between screen time and sleep disorders.

items.note: Definite-article variant of 'evidence points to'; implies a specific body of evidence without naming it
items.example: The evidence points to a systemic failure in oversight.

items.note: Recency modifier added to create freshness veneer without naming the study
items.example: Recent studies show that loneliness is a growing public health crisis.

items.note: Recency-plus-hedge variant; same gap-fill pattern
items.example: Recent research suggests that intermittent fasting may extend lifespan.

items.note: Past-perfect recency variant; all three recency forms are distinct token sequences
items.example: Recent research has found that air pollution affects cognitive development.

items.note: Novelty framing variant; 'new' is slightly stronger claim than 'recent'
items.example: New research suggests coffee may reduce the risk of Parkinson's disease.

items.note: Variant with 'studies'; same novelty-without-citation pattern
items.example: New studies show that microplastics accumulate in human tissue.

items.note: Broadened professional class as authority; no individual or body named
items.example: According to health professionals, screen time before bed disrupts sleep.

items.note: Domain-qualified unnamed attribution; appears frequently in AI health content
items.example: According to medical experts, stress is a leading cause of heart disease.

items.note: Unnamed potential arguers; AI uses to present a view without committing to it or naming anyone who holds it
items.example: Some would argue that social media has done more harm than good.

items.note: Hypothetical arguer device; AI uses to hedge its own claims as if attributing them to an unnamed third party
items.example: One could argue that the policy unfairly targets small businesses.

items.note: Softer hedge variant of 'one could argue'; same mechanism
items.example: One might argue that the benefits outweigh the risks.

items.note: Passive form of the one-could-argue device; AI uses to present contested claims without attribution
items.example: It could be argued that the current system rewards failure.

items.note: Present-tense variant of 'it could be argued'; same hedged-claim device without author
items.example: It can be argued that remote work reduces team cohesion.
